inputs.tool_used: check_table (no matching value in the technique enum, so recorded as manual)

findings.notes: Produced by check_table, recorded under technique 'manual' only because the findings schema's technique enum has no check_table value. The paper's ONLY table is reported entirely as median [Q1;Q3] on ordinal scales plus a bare n column. GRIM, GRIMMER, SPRITE and DEBIT all require a mean and SD, so the denominator here is zero: not one of the 49 cells admits a granularity check, and the tool returned 0 checks run against 49 refusals. Every median does lie inside its own reported IQR, and every value lies within the scale bounds the paper states (Garcia 18-point, Combs 9-point), so nothing is out of range - but that is the absence of a contradiction, not a verification. No validated tool in this toolkit checks the attainable-value set of a median or quartile of integer data at n=12/n=15, so the quartile granularity (values printed as .3/.8/.5) was deliberately NOT hand-derived. This is the single most important coverage fact about the paper: its tabular data is arithmetically unfalsifiable.

consequence.explanation: The 14 neurological-deficit comparisons that Table 1 carries - including the abstract's central claim that Cortexin and Cerebrolysin lowered neurological deficit - cannot be arithmetically checked from what is printed.

findings.notes: DOWNGRADED FROM THE TOOL'S 'suspicious' AND REPORTED AS NO ANOMALY. Every one of the 34 flagged repeated values (33.75, 32.25, 37.75, 44.75, 48.25, 28.75, 35.25, 47.25, 102.5 ...) terminates in .25, .5 or .75, and the flagged columns sit at a stride of exactly 5 (26/31/36/41, 58/63/68/73, 79/84/89/94). The tool's own row-pair output names the column layout: '1st d - e', '1st d - n', '1st d - nw', '1st d - se', '1st d average search time' - four quadrant-entry trials per day plus their average. The Methods confirm 'Each animal was placed in the apparatus 4 times', so every average-search-time value is a mean of four integer-second latencies and is therefore a multiple of 0.25 BY CONSTRUCTION. Its apparent 4-significant-digit precision is an artifact of dividing by 4; it carries roughly two digits of real information, and collisions among such values across 12,201 cells are expected rather than surprising. This is squarely rulebook rule 11(b). Reporting it as duplication would be a false accusation manufactured by the granularity of a derived column.

consequence.explanation: No claim is affected: the flagged values are an arithmetic property of averaging four trials, not evidence about how the data were produced.

findings.location: Linked figshare spreadsheet, Morris water maze trial columns; analysed in Fig 7 and Fig 8
findings.quote: Each animal was placed in the apparatus 4 times for a maximum of 1 min with a break between sets of 30 s. If the rat did not find the platform for 1 min, it was placed on the platform and left for 15 s, after which the training was continued according to the above-indicated pattern [[17]].

reported.analysis_stated: Kruskal-Wallis rank analysis and the Dunn post-hoc test; data shown as the mean ± SEM

inputs.source: occurrence counts reported by detect_raw_duplication over the linked figshare spreadsheet

findings.notes: The value 60.0 - the trial cutoff - occurs 1,131 times across the data file, and in individual water-maze trial columns it recurs 120, 108, 95 and 61 times. The primary cognitive outcome is therefore heavily right-censored: in several early-training columns the large majority of animals never found the platform and were assigned the ceiling. The paper nonetheless plots these as mean ± SEM (Figs 7 and 8) and analyses them with Kruskal-Wallis. A mean computed over a censored variable understates the true latency by an amount that depends on how many animals hit the cap, which differs by group and by day, so between-group mean differences in the early days are confounded with differential censoring. Kruskal-Wallis is at least rank-based and so partially robust, but the plotted means and SEMs - which are what a reader interprets - are not. Counts are read from the tool's occurrence tally; I did not independently recount them, and the exact per-column denominators were not verified because the 2.6 MB grid could not be read without sampling.

consequence.explanation: Affects the Morris water maze conclusions for both the acute (Fig 7) and chronic (Fig 8) series, which carry the abstract's claim of reduced cognitive impairment.

findings.notes: The multiplicity arithmetic returned n_tests = 0: all 14 comparisons were dropped rather than coerced, because every p is printed as a bound rather than a value. So no family-wise or false-discovery correction can be computed for this paper at all, and no surviving-claims interval can be quoted. To be fair to the authors, this is NOT a case of uncorrected testing: Dunn's post-hoc (used for the nonparametric families) and the stated Bonferroni correction (used for the ANOVA families) both do control multiplicity. The finding is that the reporting makes the correction impossible to verify, not that it is absent.

consequence.explanation: No correction arithmetic can be performed on the Table 1 family, so the multiplicity burden of the paper's main neurological result cannot be quantified either way.

findings.location: Results 3.7.1, brain necrosis volume in placebo group; n and dispersion type from the Fig 10 caption
findings.quote: During morphometry, the average volume of necrosis in the placebo group was 26 ± 5% of the size of the left hemisphere.
findings.notes: WEAK FLAG - read the caveat before using it. Both readings clear the plausibility ceiling comfortably (SD=5 is 9.4% of the maximum possible; SD=15 is 28.3%), so there is no arithmetic violation here at all. The `suspicious` verdict comes solely from the tool's preference heuristic favouring the SD reading. I judge that heuristic to be pointing the wrong way in this instance: a coefficient of variation of 19% (the SD reading) would be unusually tight for infarct volume in a filament MCAO model, where 30-50% is typical, whereas the SEM reading (SD=15, CV 58%) is the biologically ordinary one and is what the Fig 10 caption actually states. Recorded for completeness rather than as a concern. A first attempt at this call errored with a TypeError on the `decimals` argument; it was re-run without it, so the ceiling used a flat 1% margin rather than the printed precision.

consequence.explanation: Would affect only the reader's sense of spread around the 26% placebo necrosis volume; the reported group difference does not depend on which label is correct.

reported.supporting_statistics: none - no CI, no test statistic, no exact p, no stated SESOI

computed.reason: absence_of_evidence requires ci_low and ci_high; the paper reports no confidence interval for any outcome

inputs.blocked_by: no interval estimate exists anywhere in the paper

findings.notes: The tool could not be run, and that refusal is the result. The paper's headline conclusion is an equivalence claim, but no head-to-head Cortexin-versus-Cerebrolysin test is reported anywhere: both drugs were separately compared against placebo, and 'comparable effective' is inferred from both being significant against placebo. That is an affirming-the-null inference - two drugs each beating placebo does not establish that they are equivalent to each other. Because no confidence interval is reported for any outcome in this paper, the largest true difference between Cortexin and Cerebrolysin that the data still permit cannot be bounded, and no smallest effect size of interest is stated against which equivalence could be tested. The same pattern applies to the several other no-difference statements ('did not significantly differ between groups', 'p> 0.05 in each case', 'indistinguishable from the animals in placebo group').

consequence.explanation: The Conclusions' central comparative claim rests on an inference the reported statistics do not support and which cannot be checked.

inputs.source: Methods 2.13 read against the design described in Methods 2.3 and the figure captions

findings.notes: Rulebook rule 5, design validity. The study is repeatedly a groups-by-time design - Table 1 scores the same 87 rats at three timepoints; the water maze follows the same animals across four training days and, in the chronic series, across three treatment periods; rotarod and open field are measured before and after treatment in the chronic animals. The Methods list only between-groups procedures: one-way ANOVA, independent t-tests with Bonferroni, Kruskal-Wallis and Dunn. No repeated-measures ANOVA, mixed model, Friedman test or within-animal adjustment is mentioned anywhere. Treating repeated observations on the same animal as independent understates the standard errors for within-animal contrasts. Note the counter-consideration: if every reported comparison is strictly between groups at a single timepoint (which the figure captions are consistent with, since all reference marks are 'compared to Intact' or 'compared to placebo'), then the between-groups tests are appropriate at each timepoint and the problem reduces to unmodelled multiplicity across timepoints rather than a violated independence assumption. The paper does not say which, so this cannot be resolved from the text.

consequence.explanation: Bears on Table 1 and the four figure-based longitudinal outcomes (rotarod, open field, and both Morris water maze series).

findings.quote: Cortexin® receptor binding in vitro.Data shown as the median and range (n = 2).

inputs.source: Fig 14 caption from extract_xml; S2 File assay list from extract_supplement

findings.notes: The receptor-binding result reaches the Abstract and the Conclusions, and it rests on n = 2. A 'median and range' summary of two observations is uninformative - the median is just the midpoint of the two values and the range is the pair itself - yet the binding percentages are carried into the Abstract to one decimal place (80.1%, 73.5%, 49.0%, 44.0%, 39.7%), a precision the design cannot support. No dispersion, no replication beyond duplicate, and no statistical test accompanies these numbers. GRIM-percentage was deliberately NOT applied: these are percent inhibition of radioligand binding, a continuous ratio, not a share of a sample, so the granularity argument does not hold and running it would manufacture a false impossibility. Separately, S2 File documents a 28-assay panel while the narrative reports 5 targets; whether the other 23 appear in Fig 14 cannot be determined, because the figure could not be read.

consequence.explanation: The Abstract's and Conclusions' mechanistic claim that Cortexin acts on AMPA, kainate, mGluR1, GABAA1 and mGluR5 rests entirely on duplicate assays.

findings.quote: Brain content of ¹²⁵I-labeled Cortexin®, Cerebrolysin® and albumin in mice.Data shown as geometric mean (n = 15).

inputs.source: Fig 13 caption and Methods 2.10 from extract_xml

findings.notes: The Methods are explicit that 15 mice per group were split across three timepoints with 'animals (5 animals from each group) were killed by decapitation' at each of 0.5, 2 and 4 hours - a destructive sampling design, so each timepoint rests on 5 animals, not 15. The figure caption states a bare 'n = 15', which a reader will naturally take as the n behind each plotted point. Whether this is an overstatement or a legitimate statement of the group total depends on how Fig 13 is laid out, and the figure could not be read. Left INDETERMINATE rather than flagged, because resolving it requires the figure. Noted because the abstract's blood-brain-barrier claim ('concentrations equal to 6-8% of concentrations found in whole blood') derives from these points and would rest on n = 5 per timepoint.

consequence.explanation: Bears on the precision behind the Abstract's blood-brain-barrier penetration claim, but cannot be resolved without seeing the figure.

unchecked.location: Figs 3-14 (all quantitative results other than Table 1)
unchecked.reason: Every numeric outcome in this paper apart from the Table 1 neurological scores exists ONLY as a bar or line in a figure. The group means, SEMs and ns behind Figs 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 12, 13 and 14 are printed nowhere in the text, the table or the supplements. No forensic tool can reach them without reading pixels, which would be tier-2 provenance barred from GRIM/GRIMMER/SPRITE/DEBIT anyway. This is the largest single blind spot in this review: the antioxidant panel (7 outcomes), both water-maze series, rotarod, open field, adhesive latency and hippocampal morphometry were all left unchecked for this reason.

unchecked.location: Linked figshare spreadsheet, cell-by-cell typed sweep of all 12,201 numeric cells
unchecked.reason: extract_supplement returned 2,600,690 characters across 124,730 lines, which exceeds what can be read without sampling by line offset. Per the brief, a check built on a sampled table is worse than no check, so no per-cell parse_cells_typed/check_table sweep was attempted. The file was NOT left unswept, however: detect_raw_duplication loaded the entire grid itself and covered all 12,201 numeric cells across all 3 sheets, and only the header region was read directly (to confirm the column layout on which the duplication verdict depends).

unchecked.location: Table 1 quartile granularity (Q1/Q3 values printed as .3, .5, .8 for n=12 and n=15 integer-scale data)
unchecked.reason: The attainable-value set of a quartile of integer data at a given n is constrained, and the printed values are suggestive of a specific interpolation convention. But no validated tool in this toolkit checks median or quartile granularity - GRIM, GRIMMER, SPRITE and DEBIT all require a mean and an SD. Deliberately NOT hand-derived: computing the attainable quartile set myself would be exactly the unauditable arithmetic the brief forbids.

unchecked.location: Brain necrosis volume, effect size of the 45% and 38% reductions (Results 3.7.1)
unchecked.reason: check_effect_plausibility was considered and rejected. Only the placebo mean (26 +/- 5%, n=9) is printed; the Cortexin and Cerebrolysin group means are given only as relative reductions ('smaller by 45% and 38%') and their dispersions appear only in Fig 10. Deriving mean2 = 26 x 0.55 and inventing an SD would be fabricating the tool's inputs, so no effect size was computed.

recalc_chi_squared could not be run. The text gives only the placebo group's breakdown ('5 of 12 ... did not find the duct tape, and 4 of 12 found it, but subsequently did not try to remove it'); the comparator group counts appear only as percentages inside Fig 3, and no chi-squared statistic or df is reported for reconstruction.

grim_percentage was considered and deliberately NOT applied. These are percent inhibition of radioligand binding - a continuous ratio measurement, not 100*k/n for an integer count of sample units. GRIM's granularity argument does not hold for them, and applying it would manufacture a false impossibility. Recorded here so the omission is a visible decision rather than a silence.

unchecked.location: All p-values in the paper, for GRIM-U rank-sum granularity
unchecked.reason: grimu_check is applicable only to Mann-Whitney U / Wilcoxon rank-sum p-values with stated group sizes. This paper uses Kruskal-Wallis with Dunn post-hoc, one-way ANOVA with Bonferroni t-tests, and chi-squared - none of which is a rank-sum test - and in any case reports no exact p-values, only thresholds. Not applicable on two independent grounds.

unchecked.location: Baseline similarity across treatment groups (csf_test / bayesian_table1_dispersion)
unchecked.reason: No baseline table exists. Table 1's 3-hour column is a post-ischemia severity measure rather than a pre-randomisation baseline, it is reported as median/IQR rather than mean/SD/n, and no baseline p-values are printed anywhere. Neither the Carlisle-Stouffer-Fisher test nor the Table 1 dispersion test has the inputs it requires.

verify_power_analysis could not be run because the paper states no power calculation, no target power, no assumed effect size and no sample-size justification anywhere. Group sizes of 12-15 per arm across 7 arms are asserted without rationale. The absence is itself the reporting finding.

Not applicable: the paper contains exactly one table, and its cells are median [Q1;Q3], not the (mean, SD) pairs detect_duplication compares. Several Table 1 cells are identical across groups (for example '4 [3;4]' appears in four different treatment rows in the Combs 3 h column), but on a 9-point integer scale with n=12 and near-identical post-ischemia severity, identical medians and IQRs are the expected result of a tight bounded distribution (rulebook 11c) and were not flagged.

unchecked.location: S2 File in vitro binding assay table (28 rows x 7 columns)
unchecked.reason: Swept and found to contain no checkable statistics. Every cell is a protocol parameter - assay source, radioligand, ligand concentration, Kd, non-specific binding compound, incubation time - not a study result. No forensic technique applies to a methods-conditions table.

Considered and skipped as uninformative rather than run for appearance. The group sizes (15/12/12/12/12/12/12; 10/9/9/9; 15/13/15/14/15/13/15) and the 224 total are not round numbers under any modulus the tool tests, so the check could only return a null result.
